Entered at the post-office at Medora, Dak., as second class mail matter.

articles.text: The law recently passed increasing the membership of Dakota's Council to twenty-four; and the House of Representatives to forty-eight, is meeting the universal favor of press and people. It had become a matter of necessity, owing to our largely increased population.
articles.summary: Dakota legislature enlarged; editor approves.

articles.text: Stockmen of Montana, not satisfied with their attempt at trying to keep out all outsiders by the report that the ranges are full, are now buying land of the government and railroad company. They are beginning to realize the fact that their dog-in-the-manger style will not work.
articles.summary: Montana stockmen buying government and railroad land.

articles.text: All things considered, it would have been hard for the Republicans to have bettered the ticket. Blaine and Logan will undoubtedly be elected. There is a strong feeling, especially among business men, that the country would be more prosperous under Arthur, but there are few Republicans who will not enter into the campaign with a vim. Blaine will scarcely attempt as President, what he came nearly making a failure of as secretary of State.—his Peruvian scheme.
articles.summary: Comment on the Republican ticket of Blaine and Logan.

articles.text: The mind of the stockman is happy. To say that cattle are looking well does not express it. It is well-known that cattle are by no means at their best during this season but one would think from their looks that they are all stall-fed cattle. The per cent. of calves is smaller than was expected, it not reaching much over 75 per cent. in the most favorable cases. This is made up for in the splendid condition of the cattle and the small per cent. of loss. The latter in no case has reached 3 per cent. and oftener has gone way below that.
articles.summary: Cattle in the Bad Lands in fine condition; calf crop about 75 per cent, losses under 3 per cent.

articles.text: A constant source of wonderment is the vast drain of cattle from Minnesota and Iowa to Dakota and Montana and that the supply seems practically inexhaustible. A low estimate would be 50,000 one's and two's that have been shipped to this country from the above mentioned states this season. This movement of stock means far more to our future cattle trade than an outsider would suppose. A grade animal is worth $10 to $20 more as a four-year-old than is native or Texan stock. Almost every one of the Minnesota and Iowa cattle are graded. To be sure some of them are low grade, but blood will tell and tell strongly when the cattle are sold. Our cattlemen have also awaked to the advantage of using full-blood bulls and they are being universally used in the Bad Lands. This will increase the value of the herds very materially and raise the standard of our cattle even above its present high plane.
articles.summary: Graded cattle from Minnesota and Iowa and full-blood bulls are raising the standard of Bad Lands herds.

articles.text: An article in the Pioneer-Press again calls to mind a subject of which we have before written and which can only be remedied by a united action among the different cattle associations. It is in reference to persons selling diseased stock to avoid a total loss or keeping it until it dies, although it may communicate the disease to fifty others before death. We again wish to call attention to the system practiced in Germany, by which every diseased animal is taken before an inspector and killed if pronounced incurable. The owner in this case receives about two-thirds the value of the animal, while a severe fine is visited upon him in case he conceals the fact of the disease. This plan has worked very satisfactorily and has been found to be the only way by which disease can be eradicated. In conjunction with other stock organizations, this should be one of the first matters toward which to turn our attention. Its manifest feasibility should commend itself especially to stock-raising states and territories and a combined effort of the several associations could get laws passed which would prevent the spread of any disease. The expenses would be light, almost nothing in comparison to the loss should an epidemic start among our cattle. Each district could have an inspector, working in conjunction with an association, who could pronounce on every case of sickness. We hope this matter will be agitated by cattle papers until definite action is taken upon it by the associations and through them, by the different legislatures.
articles.summary: Editor urges a German-style inspection system to stamp out diseased stock.

articles.text: Now that the question of opening the Sioux reservation has been set at rest, for a year at least, there will be no delay in pushing the Medora & Black Hills R. R. to completion. Even were the reservation opened it is extremely probable that no move would be made by the North-Western toward building into the Hills, on account of the expense of crossing the Missouri. The bridge would cost as much or more than did the N. P. bridge, which would be nearly half what the completed road would cost from Medora to the Hills terminus. Already orders have been given for the survey of the road and we are assured by the Marquis de Mores that the stage route, which will be in full operation inside of three weeks is a mere preliminary to the railroad. These matters all take considerable time, but "let patience have her perfect work" and we will soon see the realization of all the present plans toward developing this country. There is an abundance of capital back of all these plans but outside capitalists see their certainty of success and are joining forces with the present company.
articles.summary: With the Sioux reservation closed, the Medora & Black Hills railroad will be pushed; the Marquis de Mores says the stage route will run within three weeks.

articles.text: At the New York horse show Cyrus W. Field received the first prize for matched pair. Fred. Gebhard's Leo received the first prize for hunters' mare or gelding, also the special prize.—[Black Hills Pioneer.
articles.summary: New York horse show prizes to Cyrus W. Field and Fred. Gebhard (from the Black Hills Pioneer).

articles.text: The grass-feeding animals of Colorado to-day are worth in dollars fifty millions. This will be increased ten millions, at least, the present year, by the calf, colt and lamb crop, and by the importation of animals from other States.—[Live-Stock Record.
articles.summary: Value of Colorado grazing stock (from the Live-Stock Record).

articles.text: The contract for furnishing cattle to the Indians at Standing Rock will probably be awarded to J. B. Martin, of Prairie du Chien, who bid $27. This is a doubtful experiment on the part of the government and will doubtless result in the cattle all being killed during the coming winter.
articles.summary: Standing Rock Indian beef contract likely to go to J. B. Martin of Prairie du Chien at $27.

articles.text: Cattle are now accumulating flesh so rapidly that the process of growing is fairly visible to the eye. In a short time there will be an abundance of beeves. The survivors of the past winter's hardships have forgotten their sufferings, and are now contented, happy and growing fat speedily.—[Kansas Cowboy.
articles.summary: Cattle fattening fast after the winter (from the Kansas Cowboy).

articles.text: There is a scheme on foot in Denver to hold a great live stock fair there next year in connection with the mineral, manufacturing and agricultural exposition. If such an exhibition is held, Denver is essentially the point for it, as being nearer the center of the great stock section of the country than any city that could make such an exhibition practicable. It should receive the encouragement of the stock growers of the west and the support of the business men of Denver.—[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Proposed live stock fair at Denver (from the N. M. Stock Grower).

articles.text: Tom Sun, of Rawlins, Wyo., with his family, was in the city the past week. He says the Sweetwater, on which his range is located near Devil's Gate, is higher than known for eleven years. The grass on the range is thicker and better than ever known, and the calf crop simply surprising. The extra number of bulls that have been placed upon the range are accountable for the gratifying increase, and have demonstrated the wisdom of the rule requiring each stockmen to fully provide himself with male beasts.—[Cheyenne Live-Stock Journal.
articles.summary: Tom Sun of Rawlins, Wyo., reports good range on the Sweetwater (from the Cheyenne Live-Stock Journal).

articles.text: Colts should be halter-broken while following their dams; they never forget it. Once broken always broken. Youngsters may be weaned from their dams at six months old. They should be fed with oats and wheat bran when taken from their mother's milk; it will keep them growing through the first winter, which is essential to early maturity. The good start lays the foundation, in bone and substance, for a good horse. Any check to the growth of the young scion the first winter will seldom be recovered in after years. A colt neglected the first winter never recovers its proper shape, nor does it grow the size and strength of body and limbs which naturally appertain to his breed.—[Kansas L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Advice on breaking and weaning colts (from the Kansas L. S. Indicator).

articles.text: Never, in the history of the live-stock business of Texas, has there been such buying and selling and interchange of stock as there has been for the past month, and likely to continue for at least two weeks to come. It would seem as though every large ranchman and every heavy buyer in the region west of the Mississippi had gone there to buy or to make contracts for the future. The trail is full of moving herds, and for weeks past every railroad in the State has been having a rush. Rolling stock is at a premium, and on some of the roads cars could not be had under any circumstances. It is not that cars are limited in number, but that large lots of cattle are being shipped. The trade in horses has been unusually large also. About twenty car-loads have been shipped to the vicinity of Wichita Falls, Kan., and some east. Most of the cattle go north and west.—[Arizona Live-Stock Journal.
articles.summary: Heavy cattle trading in Texas (from the Arizona Live-Stock Journal).

articles.text: A ranchman named Wilson, of Colorado, now said to be worth some $2,000,000 to $3,000,000, some twenty-five or thirty years ago made the trip to Pike's peak with a team or two of oxen, and which hauled himself and family and all their possessions. A short time since this adventurous settler, through a lawyer in this city, sold one of his ranches to an English company for between $400,000 and $500,000. It was a curious circumstance that first directed Mr. Wilson's attention to the capabilities of Colorado as a stock-raising state. On his way to the peak a yoke of his oxen gave out. He therefore turned them loose, as he thought, to die. A year or so afterward he was passing through the same tract of country, when he came upon his oxen, looking in splendid condition. He at once made up his mind if oxen could stand such a winter as that which this yoke had just weathered in such prime condition that stock-raising would be a profitable business in Colorado. He immediately went into the business, with the result that now "cattle upon a thousanp hills" are his, besides several ranches and a mansion in the city of Denver.—[Chicago News.
articles.summary: How Colorado ranchman Wilson got into stock-raising (from the Chicago News).

articles.text: Each recurring year Texas more nearly approaches the condition of being the nursery and breeding grounds, from which reservoir the western states and territories draw their main supply of young steers. As to this state being the most prolific breeding section, all agree, while many of our successful cattlemen hold that farther north young steers develop into larger beeves than in this latitude. The cry is often heard, "Texas ranches for cows and calves—the western territories for young steers." Well, we can for an indefinite time supply young steers, and stock cattle too, for less favored breeding grounds. With England opposing the reception of store cattle and Kansas and New Mexico hostile to the reception of Texas cattle, from fear of disease, Texans can still raise and fatten beeves for St. Louis and Chicago markets and for the dead meat markets, both foreign and at home.—[Texas L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Texas as the breeding ground for northern ranges (from the Texas L. S. Indicator).

articles.text: One of the most niggardly practices of western ranchmen is the failure to provide enough bulls. Each ranchman usually contends that he has bulls enough for his own cows, but that his neighbors are derelict, and that he does not propose to buy extra bulls for his neighbor's herd. There are a good many men mean enough to allow their cows to be served by the bulls belonging to others; not realizing that they are pursuing a very short-sighted policy; not only robbing their neighbor of actual value, but curtailing their own profits by having more cows than bulls to serve them. A bull gets about twenty to twenty-five calves a year with perfect ease. Figure what a calf is worth to you, and multiply it by twenty-five. The calculation will convince any man that he can get three to five improved bulls for the sum he loses in one year by having one bull less than he should.—[Drovers' Journal.
articles.summary: Ranchmen should provide enough bulls (from the Drovers' Journal).

articles.text: The Calgary Herald is informed by farmers south of there that the Indians are playing sad havoc among the calves. One gentleman says that out of seventy of last year's calves he has only seven left, and that a neighbor who last year had one hundred cattle can only count twenty-five. The other day a butcher, noticing that two cows had calves, and that two Sarcees were eyeing them, went over to the farmer's boy, telling him what he saw, and that he had better go at once and tell his father, who immediately sent him after the calves; and although twenty minutes had not elapsed since the butcher left them, yet when the boy got there one calf was gone and the Indians nowhere to be seen. These depredations are carried on chiefly by the young bucks, who go in parties of five and six. They will not divulge anything, and think that it is only the one who killed the animal who is amenable to the law, and that by going in parties he cannot be so easily caught.
articles.summary: Calgary Herald reports Sarcee Indians killing settlers' calves.

articles.text: Some of our ranchmen have struck a chord which could have been sounded long since to their great advantage and independence. It is simply the spaying of heifers and old cows. It is just as easy to send off to market a full-grown, fat animal, which will bring more than a steer, as to sell as surplus of the range a sorry yearling to some other fellow who makes all the profit of the growth. And it is just as easy to have an old cow go fat to market as to die poor on the prairie or in the bog. To some extent this expedient was resorted to last year on those ranges whose prolific stock had outgrown the pounds, and with results entirely satisfactory. One of our Panhandle ranches last year spayed 2,000 heifers, and this year the little experiment will be followed by the same ranch as well as others. On those ranges where the selling mania of recent times has caused an enhancement in value of heifers this may be regarded as clear waste, but to those with prospective overstock it is a means of saving grace and profit most apparent.—[Mobeetie (Tex.) Panhandle.
articles.summary: Spaying heifers and old cows on Panhandle ranges (from the Mobeetie Panhandle).

articles.text: While in North Platte, recently, the editor of the News had a pleasant interview with Messrs. John Bratt & Co., one of the largest and oldest cattle firms in western Nebraska, whose cattle find their range not only in that State, but in Wyoming and eastern Colorado. Mr. Bratt said that for years his firm had practiced putting up all the hay they could. During the last winter and spring they fed 3,125 tons of hay, and some corn; this was to bulls, cows and calves, and although the past season was unusually severe Mr. Bratt estimates the losses of his firm at not more than two per cent. "The stock business," remarked that gentleman, as he signed an order for twenty new branding irons, "has been reduced to an exact system, and as careful judgment should be exercised as that called into use in Wall street, New York. Although most of the big stockmen think it impossible, and like child's play, to feed their range stock, we consider that every ton of hay we feed will bring us back $50, and yet our range is unexcelled. We shall feed all our bulls next winter, and some of our cows and calves." Speaking of the shipments of cattle from Texas by D. Rankin & Company to Brady Island, fifty miles northwest of North Platte, Mr. Bratt said, "I consider that this stock will be worth twenty-five per cent more coming through from Texas in this way, in a few days, than if they were on the trail all summer. Being shipped in the spring, they have all the summer in which to eat, grow fat, and become acclimated." Mr. Bratt expressed himself as not at all afraid of Texas fever.—[Sterling (Col.) News.
articles.summary: John Bratt & Co. of North Platte on feeding hay to range stock (from the Sterling News).

articles.text: Bob. Roberts is in Miles City on business.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts in Miles City on business.

articles.text: Andy Corcoran, section boss at Allard, spent Sunday in town.
articles.summary: Andy Corcoran, section boss at Allard, spent Sunday in town.

articles.text: The Marquis will return for the summer with his wife, in a few days.
articles.summary: The Marquis will return for the summer with his wife in a few days.

articles.text: F. B. Allen, attorney for the company, returned to Bismarck this morning.
articles.summary: F. B. Allen, the company's attorney, returned to Bismarck.

articles.text: J. Juelfs is loading his bull teams and will "gee, haw" to-day or to-morrow.
articles.summary: J. Juelfs loading his bull teams to start freighting.

articles.text: C. L. Brinker's father is dangerously ill and he expects to leave soon to attend him.
articles.summary: C. L. Brinker's father dangerously ill.

articles.text: John Bruguier and the two families of Yankton Indians left last Saturday for Standing Rock.
articles.summary: John Bruguier and two families of Yankton Indians left for Standing Rock.

articles.text: One of Dorr Clark's bulls was injured severely while on the way here and died soon after its arrival.
articles.summary: One of Dorr Clark's bulls died after arrival.

articles.text: Train-loads of cattle are passing through nearly every day, of from twenty to twenty-five cars.
articles.summary: Cattle trains of 20 to 25 cars pass nearly daily.

articles.text: Messrs. McKenzie and O'Brien have been overrun with work since the removal of the blacksmith shop.
articles.summary: McKenzie and O'Brien busy since the blacksmith shop was removed.

articles.text: Tom Matthews came up Friday to see the round-up and returned to Mandan Monday, after a trip to Glendive.
articles.summary: Tom Matthews visited the round-up and returned to Mandan.

articles.text: Jack Bullion came in Sunday night with about thirty horses, the most of which were for use on the round-up.
articles.summary: Jack Bullion brought in about thirty horses for the round-up.

articles.text: Five or six car-loads of freight came in yesterday. This is the dullest season of the year for freight, but it will soon pick up.
articles.summary: Five or six car-loads of freight arrived.

articles.text: Howard Eaton has gone east after another lot of cattle for the Badger Cattle company. He is expected home in a few days.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton gone east for cattle for the Badger Cattle company.

articles.text: The pillow-slip dance to be given by the young ladies at the Pyramid park hotel to-night, seems destined to be a gigantic success.
articles.summary: Pillow-slip dance at the Pyramid Park hotel tonight.

articles.text: A number of fat cattle have been gathered by the round-up and sent in for slaughtering. Those killed so far are the company's cattle.
articles.summary: Fat cattle gathered by the round-up sent in for slaughter.

articles.text: While Dorr Clark was here, he partly completed arrangements for the sale of a large number of cattle to the company. He has about 10,000 for sale.
articles.summary: Dorr Clark arranging to sell cattle to the company; has about 10,000 for sale.

articles.text: "Arkansas John" loaded and pulled for Deadwood Tuesday. Next to Ford's, his is the best outfit that has been here, having a capacity of about 90,000 pounds.
articles.summary: 'Arkansas John' freight outfit left for Deadwood.

articles.text: M. L. Holley, of Minnesota, partner in the cattle firm of H. B. Wadsworth & Co., has been visiting the ranch for several days. He returned home Tuesday morning.
articles.summary: M. L. Holley of H. B. Wadsworth & Co. visited the ranch.

articles.text: W. T. Kennedy and wife will soon start for New York on a visit. Mrs. Kennedy will stay until fall. Mr. Kennedy's business will be left in charge of John Crosby.
articles.summary: W. T. Kennedy and wife going to New York; John Crosby to run his business.

articles.text: The first load of coal from the new mine in the butte east of town, was delivered Monday. It is the best vein yet opened and will supply Medora for generations to come.
articles.summary: First coal delivered from a new mine in the butte east of town.

articles.text: A. von Steiger went to St. Paul Tuesday night to complete arrangements for a stock cattle company that he is organizing. It will be run principally with foreign capital.
articles.summary: A. von Steiger to St. Paul to organize a stock cattle company.

articles.text: Gregor Lang has just received another large lot of cattle. They were all branded with his new and ingenious "triangle JP brand, which appears for the first time in this issue of the Cow Boy.
articles.summary: Gregor Lang received more cattle under his new triangle JP brand.

articles.text: Mr. Roosevelt, the young New York reformer, who has done more toward exposing the corruptness of New York politics than any other man, is visiting his ranch here, managed by Ferris & Merrifield.
articles.summary: Theodore Roosevelt visiting his ranch, managed by Ferris & Merrifield.

articles.text: Tom Hardwicke, of the Rocky Mountain show now in Minneapolis, is in town buying horses for his outfit. He reports the gospel firm, Moody & Sankey, as doing a great work among the Minneapolitan tenderfeet.
articles.summary: Tom Hardwicke of the Rocky Mountain show buying horses in town.

articles.text: All the stock horses of the company except the three stallions have been sold to A. C. Huidekoper and H. R. Tarbell. Mr. Tarbell will be manager and has already adopted a new brand that will appear in our next issue.
articles.summary: The company's stock horses sold to A. C. Huidekoper and H. R. Tarbell.

articles.text: Persons requiring any papers drawn up, such as acknowledgements, deeds, bills of sale, relinquishments, affidavits, depositions, contracts, protests or any other legal instrument, can be accommodated at the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: Legal papers can be drawn up at the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: Rev. Wm. Cooke, of Gladstone, made us a pleasant call Monday morning. He is one of the pioneer ministers of western Dakota and knows how to reach his audience. He preaches every Sunday evening at the Cantonment.
articles.summary: Rev. Wm. Cooke of Gladstone called; preaches Sundays at the Cantonment.

articles.text: It is doubtful if the county will be organized and in running order before July 1st. Mr. Hay, one of the commissioners, has been called east and will be there until about that date. For other reasons also, it has been deemed advisable to put off the organization.
articles.summary: County organization postponed until about July 1; Commissioner Hay called east.

articles.text: The round-up passed through here last Friday morning and a jollier set of boys we never expect to meet. Their work has been done thoroughly and everything moves with the precision of clock-work. The round-up promises to be satisfactory in all respects.
articles.summary: The round-up passed through town last Friday morning.

articles.text: There are a few chronic kickers here who need to be sat on. A good illustration is the report circulated so freely that we had lost the freight route when at that very time more freight was on the way for our route than at any time before. Another example is the rumor that licenses are to be $400, when the third commissioner has not yet been appointed. These croakers should be spotted and their statements taken for what they are worth.
articles.summary: Editor rebukes 'chronic kickers' spreading rumors about the freight route and $400 licenses.

articles.text: Experiments with alfalfa will be made in the Marquis' garden, some seed having arrived. Its value for feeding stock and wonderful growing properties will make its cultivation extensive provided the experiments are as successful as there is every reason to suppose they will be.
articles.summary: Alfalfa experiments planned in the Marquis' garden.

articles.text: Dorr Clark started for his ranch last Monday. Saturday, the Short-horn bulls spoken of in our last issue, arrived, and they were as fine looking a lot as we have ever seen. Mr. Clark, before leaving, left the VVV and E6 brands with us for publication and they will appear in our next issue.
articles.summary: Dorr Clark left for his ranch; his Short-horn bulls arrived; VVV and E6 brands to be published.

articles.text: The pile-driver left here without orders last Thursday afternoon and ran into the work train at Sully Springs as a result. Several cars were smashed and the engine on the pile-driver was badly wrecked. There was luckily no loss of life but Mr. Gilbert's dining cars were, "considerably shuck up like."
articles.summary: Runaway pile-driver hit the work train at Sully Springs.

articles.text: M. Kline, of Mandan, left Monday for home, after a three day's business and pleasure trip here. The boys let him off easy and mounted him on a bronco that only ran away with him four times. He seemed to enjoy the round-up, but his prediction that " the tender-foot will be sore to-morrow," was vividly fulfilled.
articles.summary: M. Kline of Mandan left after a three-day visit and a bronco ride.

articles.text: We have received a note from Dr. E. E. Ball, of Mandan, stating that on account of sickness it will be impossible for him to keep his engagement here until the last of the month. As Dr. Ball is an excellent dentist, it will be well for those suffering from poor teeth to keep an eye on his dates, which will be published in time.
articles.summary: Dentist Dr. E. E. Ball of Mandan postpones his Medora visit.

articles.text: A serious mistake was made by the N. P. coal Co. in removing the supports from their mine here. The roof is caving in, in many places and repair work will cost more than the original expense of propping. Mr. Thompson asserts that the mine is the best on the road and in view of this fact, the removal of the props was very short-sighted.
articles.summary: N. P. coal Co. mine caving in after supports were removed.

articles.text: John Hager, of Mandan, was in town Saturday. He has concluded to go into the stage line in connection with the Marquis and others. We are pleased to note this fact, as Mr. Hager is exactly the kind of a worker we need here. He has done as much, if not more than any other one man to build up Mandan, and his experience will be a valuable addition to Medora.
articles.summary: John Hager of Mandan joins the stage line with the Marquis and others.

articles.text: The man referred to in our round-up letter as having had "strawberry shortcake in his," made a special trip to town to stop his subscription. As his three months grace was just up, we would have saved him the trouble after the last issue. He is said to "have it in" for the man who wrote the article but if he will take our advice, he will leave him severely alone and pray for a cyclone to strike him instead. We hold ourselves personally responsible for every word that appears in the COW BOY and any complaint will receive proper attention.
articles.summary: A subscriber offended by the round-up letter stops his paper.

articles.headline: NOTICE OF DISSOLUTION.
articles.text:
NOTICE OF DISSOLUTION.

TO ALL WHOM IT MAY CONCERN: Be it known that on and after this 24th day of May, 1884, the partnership heretofore existing between Chas. Shaffer and John Munroe, under the firm name of Shaffer & Munroe, Plum Grove ranch, on the Little Missouri river, is dissolved by mutual consent. All indebtedness of the firm to date will be paid by John Munroe.
articles.summary: Shaffer & Munroe partnership, Plum Grove ranch, dissolved May 24, 1884; John Munroe to pay debts.
